question: In healthcare technology, what is the main goal of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI)?

options.A: Writing new programming code for hospital databases
options.B: Teaching computer science classes to student nurses
options.C: How clinicians interact with digital technology during work
options.D: Repairing broken computer hardware in the hospital ward

explanation: You got this! HCI is simply about how healthcare workers use digital tools on the job, making sure technology helps rather than frustrates you. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why can a poorly designed computer screen or software interface become a safety hazard for patients?

options.A: It distracts nurses from spending time with patients
options.B: It drains the hospital battery backup systems too quickly
options.C: It slows down internet speeds across the entire clinic
options.D: It increases the financial cost of buying hardware

explanation: Spot on! When software is clumsy and hard to navigate, nurses waste precious time fighting with menus instead of focusing on direct patient care. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h1)

question: When software uses a 'user-centered design' approach, what is prioritized above all else?

options.A: The cheapest manufacturing cost for computer screens
options.B: The most advanced programming languages available
options.C: The fastest possible internet connection speeds
options.D: The needs and workflows of the people using the system

explanation: Exactly! User-centered design means building technology around how nurses actually work on the ward every day, keeping things simple and natural. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h2)

question: When evaluating clinical software, what does usability 'efficiency' actually measure?

options.A: How many computer monitors the hospital can buy
options.B: How much electricity the nursing station computers use
options.C: How quickly a task can be completed using the system
options.D: How many lines of code are in the software program

explanation: Well done! Efficiency is all about speed and ease—how fast and smoothly you can finish a task without running into roadblocks. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h2)

question: Which interface type allows a nurse to dictate clinical notes hands-free?
explanation: Voice interfaces let users speak commands or notes, which is very useful when hands are busy or contaminated. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h3)

question: A continuous glucose monitor sending real-time data to a nurse's tablet is an example of which interface type?
explanation: Sensors worn directly on the patient's body form wearable interfaces that stream data remotely. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h3)

question: In a busy clinical setting, what does 'cognitive load' refer to?

options.A: The mental effort required to process information and use working memory
options.B: The speed at which data travels across the hospital Wi-Fi network
options.C: The weight of the computer equipment carried around on mobile carts
options.D: The total number of patients assigned to a nurse on a single shift

explanation: Spot on! Cognitive load is simply how hard your brain has to work to process information, remember tasks, and make clinical decisions. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h4)

question: A nurse is trying to calculate a drug dose, but the screen is cluttered with pop-ups, flashing icons, and tiny text. What is this poor design causing?
explanation: You got it! Cluttered screens force your brain to waste energy sorting through useless distractions, overloading your mental capacity. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the main reason hospitals use standardized usability questionnaires for electronic health records?

options.A: To test the speed of the hospital internet server cables
options.B: To measure user satisfaction and ease of use in a structured way
options.C: To calculate the financial budget for buying new computers
options.D: To check if the computer hardware is physically clean

explanation: Exactly! These questionnaires give hospitals a clear, reliable score on whether their software is actually user-friendly for nurses. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h5)

question: Why is having 'zero complaints' from nurses NOT always a sign that a hospital software program is working well?

options.A: Nurses may have given up or created workarounds instead of reporting issues
options.B: Hospital computers block all feedback messages sent by staff
options.C: Software automatically fixes its own design errors over time
options.D: Nurses prefer spending extra hours clicking through bad menus

explanation: So true! When systems are frustrating, busy nurses often just find quiet workarounds instead of wasting time filing formal complaints. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is 'alert fatigue' in a clinical environment?

options.A: Slow loading times when opening multiple patient charts at once
options.B: Physical exhaustion from standing too long at the nursing computer station
options.C: Battery failure in wireless mobile computer carts during a night shift
options.D: Desensitization to warnings caused by too many unimportant pop-up alerts

explanation: Spot on! When software constantly cries wolf with trivial pop-ups, nurses get tired of them and start ignoring all warnings—even the life-saving ones. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to prevent software-related mistakes on the ward?

options.A: Disabling all confirmation prompts to make data entry go faster
options.B: Using smart defaults that fill in safe, common choices
options.C: Limiting pop-up warnings only to true clinical hazards
options.D: Designing clear visual layouts with readable fonts

explanation: You nailed it! Confirmation prompts act as a vital safety net. Removing them just to type faster invites accidental medication or charting errors. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h6)

question: Who serves as the vital link between frontline nursing care and software developers?
explanation: Exactly right! Nurse informaticians combine real bedside nursing experience with computer science to help design better healthcare tech. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h7)

question: Why is it so important for frontline ward nurses to be involved when designing new clinical software?

options.A: Hospital accreditation rules legally require nurses to write code
options.B: They are the only staff members trained in computer programming
options.C: They understand actual daily workflows better than remote administrators
options.D: They have extra free time during their shifts to test products

explanation: Spot on! Office administrators don't face the realities of the ward. Frontline nurses know what actually works during a busy shift. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h7)

question: What is an exciting potential use of augmented reality (AR) glasses in nursing care?

options.A: Projecting vital signs and vein maps directly into the nurse's view
options.B: Automatically administering medications through wireless signals
options.C: Replacing the need for physical nursing assessments entirely
options.D: Printing paper charts without needing ink or toner cartridges

explanation: How cool is that? AR glasses overlay helpful digital patient data and vein guides right into your natural field of vision while you work. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h8)

question: How do touchless gesture controls help nurses working in sterile environments like the operating room?

options.A: They eliminate the need for patient identification wristbands
options.B: They make computer screens brighter in dark surgical suites
options.C: They allow computers to run without needing any electricity
options.D: They let nurses interact with software without breaking sterile technique

explanation: Brilliant! Gesture controls let you check screens and records with a wave of your hand, keeping your sterile gloves clean and safe. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T2#GNS113_U3_T2_h8)
